title: Manufacturing Quality Control Types and Best Practices
summary: Manufacturing quality control is critical for brands working with external manufacturers, suppliers, and fulfillment partners.
body_markdown:
Manufacturing quality control means inspecting your products and production process to prevent defects and ensure they meet predefined quality standards. It’s a system for evaluating[raw materials](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-raw-material) , components, and finished products against quality requirements.


According to[PwC’s 2025 Customer Experience Survey](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/consulting/business-transformation/library/2025-customer-experience-survey.html) , more than half of consumers have stopped buying from a brand because of a bad experience with its products or services. An effective quality control plan is what keeps those products from leaving the manufacturing floor in the first place.


Learn more about manufacturing quality control, the quality control methods used across industries, and the best practices to implement effective systems within your workflow.


## What is manufacturing quality control?


Manufacturing quality control uses data collection, physical inspections, and product quality testing to identify defects during production and confirm that every item meets specified requirements. Rather than only hunting for defects, effective QC is about validating the positive traits that define your brand’s value. Here are a few examples:


-


**Consistency.** Ensuring a custom-dyed linen shirt matches your Pantone shade across every fabric lot, preventing color variations that trigger returns.


-


**Reliability.** Verifying that a consumer electronics device holds a charge and functions properly during its life cycle.


-


**Safety and compliance.** Confirming that a silicone kitchen spatula can withstand heat up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit without degrading, keeping your product safe and compliant with food safety standards.


Effective quality control measures are also a[competitive advantage](https://www.shopify.com/blog/competitive-advantage) . Consistency builds trust, while a single quality miss is one of the fastest ways to lose a customer for good. In Attentive’s[2026 State of Loyalty & Retention](https://www.attentive.com/blog/loyalty-retention-report-2026) report, 41% of consumers named low product quality as a top reason they wouldn’t return to a brand after a first purchase. And 45% of consumers said great product quality is exactly what brings them back.


### Quality assurance vs. quality control: What’s the difference?


Although the terms quality control and quality assurance are often used interchangeably, they’re two halves of the same quality management system:


-


**Quality assurance (QA) is process-oriented.** It focuses on preventing defects by designing standard operating procedures, training factory workers, and setting up the overall manufacturing workflow.[Quality assurance](https://www.shopify.com/blog/quality-assurance) is the plan.


-


**Quality control (QC) is product-oriented.** It focuses on detecting defects by executing physical checks, weighing items, or running lab tests on finished goods. QC is checking that the plan worked.


With outsourced manufacturing, you may assume the manufacturer handles quality control. In reality, factories’ default internal QC standards are tuned to protect their margins and output, not necessarily your[brand reputation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/brand-reputation) . If products reach customers with defects, your brand typically absorbs returns, negative reviews, and any reputation hits. In other words, if you sell it, you own the quality.


When working with third-party suppliers, independent quality control workers, or external quality control inspectors, align on the acceptance criteria. These are the rules that define what makes a product acceptable versus defective. You don’t have to set these standards from scratch, but you’re ultimately responsible for signing off on them. Your agreed-upon quality requirements dictate how partners execute the inspection process, manage production equipment, and monitor process parameters.

## Types of manufacturing quality control


- Incoming inspections
- In-process inspections
- Final inspections
- Container loading inspections


Depending on your business model, you can use these QC methods separately, or combine them to ensure your product quality meets your requirements:


### Incoming inspections


An incoming inspection focuses on inspecting raw materials and components as they arrive at your workspace—whether that is a manufacturing plant, a third-party warehouse, or your home office. Quality control workers test these inputs against specific acceptance criteria to ensure no substandard components enter the production process.


If you sell glass-jar candles, for example, your acceptance criteria for incoming glassware might reject:


-


Any jar with a visible crack


-


Glass thickness varying by more than a millimeter


-


A mouth diameter that prevents the lid from sealing flush


Measurable baselines like these mean you don’t waste wax and fragrance oil pouring candles into jars you need to throw away.


### In-process inspections


Also known as production quality control, this method means continuous monitoring of goods as they move through each production stage.


If you run your own workshop, that might mean pausing to check tool calibration or inspecting the first unit to confirm the setup is right. With an outsourced manufacturing partner, it could be a checkpoint where the factory must send high-resolution photos, a video, or a pre-production sample from a test run.


Verifying that these initial units match your design specs before the factory greenlights the remaining items keeps a minor calibration error from ruining your entire order. Depending on the complexity of your product, this phase can also use advanced technology to eliminate human error, for instance:


-


**Automated inspection systems.** These systems use high-speed cameras and sensors on the assembly line to photograph and scan every item. If a label is crooked or a bottle isn’t filled to the exact line, the system automatically flags and removes it.


-


**Coordinate measuring machines (CMMs).** For highly technical products, CMMs use an ultra-precise probe to measure a 3D physical object down to the micrometer. This ensures custom-molded parts—like the interlocking gears of a watch or the metal threads of a bicycle pedal—match your technical design specs.


### Final inspections


A final inspection happens once 100% of your run is fully manufactured, and at least 80% is packaged. This threshold is the industry standard for what inspection firms call a final random inspection or pre-shipment inspection. The global testing company SGS[defines it the same way](https://www.sgs.com/en/services/final-random-inspection) , timing the check for once production is fully complete and the bulk of goods are packed and ready to dispatch.


Inspectors check finished goods for cosmetic defects, basic functionality, and the correct packaging. Because checking every item is often impossible, this phase relies on acceptance sampling. This is a statistical method where inspectors test a set percentage of the batch to determine if the entire shipment is accepted or rejected.


Say a factory produces 10,000 custom phone cases. Inspecting each one would be expensive and slow, so the quality control plan—drawing on the[industry-standard AQL sampling tables](https://asq.org/quality-resources/z14-z19) —has the inspector randomly pull and test 200 of them.


Working at General Inspection Level II and an Acceptable Quality Limit of 1.5 with seven or fewer defects means all 10,000 are accepted and shipped. Eight or more and the whole run is rejected, and the factory must halt the shipment and rework the inventory.


### Container loading inspections


This is the final line of defense before your goods leave the factory floor. This check ensures that your finished, approved products are correctly packed, labeled with the right barcodes, and safely loaded into shipping containers.


For ecommerce brands, a container loading inspection can prevent costly logistics headaches. These could be crushed boxes, water damage during transit, or inventory being rejected by your[third-party logistics (3PL)](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/third-party-logistics-3pl) provider due to missing warehouse labels.

## Best practices for manufacturing quality control


- Set clear product specs and inspection checklists
- Move to continuous quality integration
- Halt production instead of shipping flawed goods
- Connect physical quality checks to your digital operations


Integrating quality processes into your regular operations requires clear systems, direct communication, and active data collection. Use these best practices to build an effective quality control plan:


### Set clear product specs and inspection checklists


Create detailed documentation procedures that outline every specified requirement for your item. Include:


-


Physical dimensions with acceptable tolerance margins


-


Material weights, color codes, and strength requirements


-


A step-by-step inspection process checklist for quality control workers to follow


-


Acceptance criteria that define what constitutes a minor, major, or critical defect


Manufacturing errors may initially feel like an unsolvable mystery.


“We didn’t know any of the steps on how you make sure that you get quality,” Dan Demsky, co-founder of[Unbound Merino](https://unboundmerino.com/) , said on[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/unbound-merino-scaling-to-one-hundred-million-lifetime-revenue) . “We were so paranoid that we were going to mess it up because you hear a lot of horror stories. You put it in your order and then it doesn’t come to spec or it’s lower quality and then you’re out of business.”


Driven by that anxiety, Dan and his partners flew to China to stand on the factory floor themselves. They learned quality isn’t a guessing game but rather the result of comprehensive and documented procedures.


You don’t have to fly around the world for this level of control. You can establish it from your desk by sending your manufacturer two documents before production begins: a[product brief](https://www.shopify.com/blog/product-brief) and an inspection checklist. Clear documentation procedures and acceptance criteria set out in advance let you align with your manufacturer’s existing quality systems early when changes are relatively cheap.


### Move to continuous quality integration


Integrated quality control means incorporating testing throughout the product life cycle, rather than treating it as a final hurdle at the end of an assembly line. In practice, this means QC starts in the design phase and continues long after a product launch. For example, if you’re developing a waterproof backpack:


-


**In research and development (R&D).** You test fabric samples for water resistance and seam strength before finalizing patterns.


-


**During production.** You conduct mid-run checks to ensure the waterproof zippers are correctly stitched.


-


**Post-launch.** You track customer return data and reviews. If buyers report, say, a zipper failing after six months, you feed that quality data back into your design loop to upgrade the hardware for the next production run.


This continuous improvement mindset requires leadership commitment and regular, transparent communication with your factory partners to maintain manufacturing quality. On[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/life-is-good-optimism-on-demand) , Tom Hassell, president of apparel brand[Life is Good](https://lifeisgood.com/) , highlights this approach when discussing how his quality team evaluates internal printing operations alongside overseas factories.


“On a practical level, we have a quality team that historically made sure that the overseas factories were producing quality goods,” Tom says. “Now that quality team treats our own internal factory as yet one additional factory that they get to examine the products and make sure that we are shipping a quality product.”


He notes that whenever the company introduces a new fabric or color, it puts the garment through a rigorous process to ensure it will perform through 15 trips to the washer and dryer.


### Halt production instead of shipping flawed goods


If quality problems arise mid-production, consider halting operations rather than pushing flawed items to market. Refusing to compromise on your acceptance criteria may cost you in the short term, but it protects your long-term[brand credibility](https://www.shopify.com/blog/brand-credibility) .


The cost of letting a bad batch slip is high. PwC’s 2025[Customer Experience Survey](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/consulting/commercial-excellence/library/2025-customer-experience-survey.html) found that 52% of customers abandon a brand after just one poor product experience. Pausing shipment instead of distributing flawed products is how you protect that[customer’s lifetime value](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-customer-lifetime-value) .


On[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/hedley-and-bennett-scaling-through-product-development-with-customers) , Ellen Bennett, founder of the kitchen gear brand[Hedley & Bennett](https://www.hedleyandbennett.com/) , describes this scenario while discussing the inspection process required to scale the company’s product lines. Where a typical manufacturer might pull a generic design from a supplier’s catalog, Ellen’s team spent years collaborating with industrial designers and chefs to tool custom silicone ladles and spatulas from scratch.


“We did all of this, and when we were ready to ship, we realized that there was some issue with the back of the handle and we stopped production,” she says. “We stopped the shipping and had an entire batch—that was our first batch—stopped and discarded and we started over, because of that issue with the back of the tool. So that’s an example of what it takes to maintain quality, how to build a product in a way that’s with longevity.”


### Connect physical quality checks to your digital operations


Integrating your physical checks with a digital quality management system lets you monitor inspections, measure quality performance, and control inventory availability in real time. In practice, a digital system coordinates your workflow at three critical touchpoints:


-


**Monitoring active inspections.** Instead of wondering if an order is ready, track where a production run stands in the inspection queue, seeing real-time pass-or-fail results.


-


**Measuring long-term supplier performance.** A digital system aggregates your inspection data over time, tracking key performance metrics like your manufacturer’s historical defect rate. This gives you concrete data when negotiating terms or deciding whether to switch suppliers.


-


**Controlling inventory availability.** When a shipment arrives at your warehouse, the system automatically routes the stock into an unavailable digital state (like “quality control”). This prevents you from accidentally selling unverified or potentially defective products until the inventory is formally cleared.


Tracking this data doesn’t require complex software. You can log raw inspection results—like total units checked, defect counts, and error types—in a spreadsheet. From there, calculate metrics like:


-


**Acceptance rate.** The percentage of received items that successfully pass your inspection checklist.


-


**Rejected quantity.** The total number of units that fail to meet your quality requirements within a specific batch.


-


**Rejection rate.** The percentage of total produced goods turned away due to quality issues.


Consistently monitoring these metrics helps you identify trends in manufacturing performance, giving you the data required to negotiate better terms, hold factories accountable, or switch suppliers if quality drops.


## Manufacturing quality control FAQ


### What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?


Quality control focuses on the product itself, using inspections, testing, and data collection to identify defects in finished goods or production runs. Quality assurance takes a broader, process-oriented approach. It establishes the quality management system, documentation procedures, and operational guidelines to prevent defects.


### What are the main types of quality control?


The main quality control methods include inspections of incoming raw materials, in-process inspections to monitor production equipment and process parameters, and final inspection protocols for finished products. You can also use statistical quality control methods—like acceptance sampling and control charts—to evaluate batch quality without manually checking every single unit produced.


### How do ecommerce businesses manage manufacturing quality?


Manage quality by creating product specification sheets, providing suppliers with inspection checklists, and hiring independent quality control inspectors or quality control workers to review goods before shipment. Track unverified shipments by marking them “unavailable” in your ecommerce admin, so nothing sells before inspection, then monitor supplier defect and acceptance rates to hold manufacturing partners accountable.
